questions.stem: A 74-year-old man presented with 2 days of watery diarrhea and 1 day of large fluid-filled skin lesions. He had a history of cirrhotic liver disease. He had recently returned from a fishing trip on the US Gulf Coast. He had been swimming in the hotel pool but not the sea. On examination he was dehydrated, his temperature was 38.3°C, blood pressure 88/52mmHg, heart rate 115 beats/minute. Investigations: Blood cultures: curved gram-negative rods seen on microscopy
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely infective cause?
questions.explanation: Vibrio vulnificus This patient has acquired systemic Vibrio vulnificus infection following the ingestion of seafood in the US Gulf coast. Patients with cirrhosis or hemochromatosis are particularly susceptible to systemic infection and have a high mortality rate, ranging from 40% to 90%. They can present with fever and hypotension, developing bullous lesions and cellulitis. This patient is bacteremic with Vibrio as evidenced by the curved gram-negative rods indicative of Vibrio vulnificus and other Vibrio spp. Patients with a presumptive diagnosis of V. vulnificus septicemia should be started immediately on antibiotic therapy and managed aggressively in an intensive care unit. A tetracycline plus a third-generation cephalosporin is recommended.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q10

questions.model_answer: Vibrio vulnificus. Iron-overload states such as hemochromatosis are a classic risk factor (the organism sequesters iron from saturated transferrin/hemoglobin), and septicemia with rapidly evolving hemorrhagic bullae typically follows raw-oyster ingestion within 1-3 days.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA, given IVDU/incarceration) (2) beta-hemolytic streptococci (e.g. Streptococcus pyogenes).
b) Doxycycline PO monotherapy - covers CA-MRSA and streptococci and is highly active against V. vulnificus.
c) (1) Ceftriaxone IV once daily PLUS ciprofloxacin PO BID (fluoroquinolone + third-generation cephalosporin are highly active against V. vulnificus and the cipro-cefotaxime combination is synergistic); add MRSA cover if not otherwise provided. (2) Ceftriaxone IV once daily PLUS trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole PO BID (ceftriaxone covers Vibrio/strep, TMP-SMX covers MRSA).
d) (1) Aeromonas hydrophila (2) Mycobacterium marinum (3) Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (4) Streptococcus iniae (5) Shewanella species (also Photobacterium damselae, Vibrio parahaemolyticus/alginolyticus).
questions.beyond_mandell: Common purulent-cellulitis pathogens, oral MRSA regimens and the non-Vibrio marine SSTI organisms are from IDSA SSTI guidance; only the V. vulnificus drug activity/synergy is grounded in the chapter.

questions.model_answer: a) Purulent cellulitis is predominantly staphylococcal: (1) Staphylococcus aureus (the commonest, including MRSA) and (2) group A streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes); in direct-sampling series S. aureus (~50%) and GAS (~25%) account for >75% of isolates. b) Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID as single best oral agent – it covers CA-MRSA/MSSA, streptococci, and is first-line for V. vulnificus (tetracyclines are the recognized first-line anti-Vibrio drug). c) (1) Ceftriaxone IV once daily PLUS doxycycline PO BID (ceftriaxone/3rd-gen cephalosporin covers streptococci and Vibrio, doxycycline covers MRSA and Vibrio); (2) Levofloxacin PO/IV once daily PLUS trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole PO BID (levofloxacin covers Vibrio and streptococci, TMP-SMX covers MRSA) – ciprofloxacin is the listed Vibrio alternative. d) (1) Vibrio parahaemolyticus (2) Vibrio alginolyticus (3) Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (4) Mycobacterium marinum (5) Aeromonas hydrophila (Streptococcus iniae and Edwardsiella tarda are also acceptable).
questions.beyond_mandell: The IV-once-daily / PO-twice-daily combination regimens in part c are constructed to the question's constraints; Mandell grounds doxycycline + 3rd-generation cephalosporin (or ciprofloxacin) for Vibrio but does not specify these exact dual regimens.

questions.question: Aeromonas hydrophila is isolated with the following susceptibilities: ampicillin (R), ceftriaxone (R), aztreonam (R), meropenem (R), ertapenem (R), tigecycline (S). The organism possessed a carbapenemase that was inactivated by EDTA.
questions.question_raw:
Q39 (2018)
Aeromonas hydrophilia organism with the following susceptibilities: Ampicillin (R), Ceftriaxone (R), Aztreonam (R), Meropenem (R), Ertapenem (R), Tigecycline (S)

parts.text: Which class of carbapenemases is represented here?

parts_raw.text: A) The organism possessed a carbapenemase which was inactivated by EDTA. Which class of carbapenemases is represented here?

questions.model_answer: Ambler Class B metallo-beta-lactamases (MBLs). They require zinc at the active site, so the chelating agent EDTA sequesters zinc and inactivates the enzyme (e.g. NDM-1, of the type described in carbapenem-resistant Vibrio fluvialis).
questions.beyond_mandell: The EDTA/zinc mechanism and Ambler classification are established microbiology; the chapter supports MBL (NDM-1) carbapenem resistance in a related Vibrio.

cohort_answer.text: Class B metallo-beta-lactamases. EDTA is the chelating agent of zinc in the active site

questions.model_answer: Cellulitis without sepsis: (1) doxycycline or (2) a fluoroquinolone (e.g. ciprofloxacin) - both highly active against V. vulnificus. If sepsis/necrotizing fasciitis: immediate surgical consultation with debridement of all devitalized tissue (or amputation) PLUS a third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone) combined with doxycycline (or minocycline) or ciprofloxacin; the ciprofloxacin-cefotaxime combination is synergistic.

cohort_answer.text: Cellulitis without sepsis/nec fasc: Doxy or Cipro. For sepsis/nec fasc: immediate surgical debridement, combination of Ceftriaxone with Doxy or Cipro

questions.model_answer:
a) Vibrio vulnificus (rapidly progressive necrotizing cellulitis with hemorrhagic bullae after seawater/shell-wound exposure).
b) Early antibiotics are critical plus immediate surgical consultation for debridement of devitalized tissue. Mild-moderate: doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone monotherapy. Severe/bacteremic/necrotizing: a third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) PLUS doxycycline (or minocycline) or ciprofloxacin, with surgical debridement; cipro-cefotaxime is synergistic.

cohort_answer.text: Vibrio vulnificus (exposure to salt water of puncture wounds, incubation 3-7 days). Treatment: mild-moderate - monotherapy with tetracycline or FQ x5-7d; severe or bacteremic - doxy + ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (IDSA); debridement of devitalized tissue or amputation may be lifesaving; FQ/3rd gen ceph/doxy highly active, cipro+cefotaxime synergistic

questions.question: A cirrhotic man floated for 2 days in seawater around New Orleans. He presents with fever and bullous leg lesions and is bacteremic with curved gram-negative bacilli.

parts.text: Name two possible organisms.
Describe treatment.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 possible organisms
Describe tx

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Vibrio vulnificus (most likely: cirrhosis plus warm-seawater exposure with rapidly necrotizing bullous cellulitis). (2) Photobacterium damselae (formerly V. damselae) - causes serious wound infections with a clinical picture reminiscent of V. vulnificus; other Vibrio spp. (e.g. V. alginolyticus, which has caused necrotizing fasciitis) are alternatives.
b) Immediate surgical consultation for debridement of all devitalized tissue (or amputation), as this can be lifesaving; combined with early antibiotics because cellulitis advances rapidly. Use a third-generation cephalosporin plus doxycycline (or a fluoroquinolone); the combination of a third-generation cephalosporin with minocycline/ciprofloxacin improved survival in V. vulnificus necrotizing fasciitis, and ciprofloxacin-cefotaxime showed synergy. Supportive care for sepsis/shock.

cohort_answer.text: Vibrio vulnificus, Vibrio parahaemolyticus (GI illness predominant), Vibrio alginolyticus (nec fasc reported). Treatment: urgent surgical debridement, 3rd gen ceph + FQ/Doxy (Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily + Doxy 100mg PO BID or Cipro 500mg PO BID)

questions.model_answer:
a) Clostridium septicum.
b) (1) Gram-positive (may appear gram-variable) rods. (2) Terminal/subterminal spores giving a swollen "drumstick" appearance.
c) Colonic (gastrointestinal) malignancy - spontaneous C. septicum myonecrosis/bacteremia is strongly associated with occult colorectal carcinoma.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA); (2) streptococci — group A and groups C, F, G ("skin popping" injection-drug-use cellulitis of extremities/neck).
b) Doxycycline (a tetracycline) — tetracyclines are first-line for Vibrio vulnificus soft tissue infection; often combined with a third-generation cephalosporin.
c) Using agents other than doxycycline, both with marine/Vibrio activity: (1) Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV once daily (third-generation cephalosporin); (2) Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO twice daily (or levofloxacin 750 mg PO once daily). Vibrio spp. are susceptible in vitro to third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones.
d) (1) Vibrio vulnificus (also V. parahaemolyticus, V. alginolyticus, non-O1 V. cholerae — saltwater/seafood); (2) Aeromonas hydrophila (fresh water); (3) Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (erysipeloid — saltwater fish/shellfish handlers); (4) Mycobacterium marinum (aquaria, fish); (5) Vibrio parahaemolyticus.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort gives ciprofloxacin as the single Vibrio drug; Mandell makes tetracyclines (doxycycline) first-line with cefotaxime/ciprofloxacin only as alternatives, so doxycycline is the preferred single agent.

cohort_answer.text: Pathogens: GAS, S. aureus. Vibrio drug: Ciprofloxacin. Alternative regimens: IV CRO + doxy, or CRO + levofloxacin (can also use ceftazidime as 3rd gen ceph but dosing frequency 3x daily). Marine-borne agents: Vibrio vulnificus, Plesiomonas sp., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Mycobacterium marinum, Aeromonas hydrophila, Shewanella spp. (family Vibrionaceae), Streptococcus iniae, Burkholderia pseudomallei.

c) (1) Cirrhosis/underlying liver disease (2) Iron-overload states (hemochromatosis, hemolytic anemia, chronic renal failure) (3) Malignancy, HIV infection, or immunosuppressive medications.
d) (1) Norovirus (2) Hepatitis A virus.
questions.beyond_mandell: The two oyster-associated viruses (norovirus, hepatitis A) are established general knowledge, not from this chapter.

questions.model_answer:
a) Water exposure: Aeromonas - fresh/brackish water; Burkholderia pseudomallei - fresh water/wet soil; Vibrio vulnificus - warm salt/brackish seawater (or raw oysters); Streptococcus iniae - fresh water (tilapia/fish handling); Mycobacterium marinum - fresh or salt water (aquariums, fish); Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - salt water (fish/shellfish handling).
b) Clinical syndrome: Aeromonas - cellulitis, myonecrosis, ecthyma gangrenosum; B. pseudomallei - melioidosis (skin abscesses/ulcers, pneumonia, sepsis, worse in cirrhotics/diabetics); V. vulnificus - rapidly progressive necrotizing cellulitis with hemorrhagic bullae, primary septicemia; S. iniae - cellulitis/bacteremia; M. marinum - indolent papules/nodules with sporotrichoid spread ('fish-tank granuloma'); E. rhusiopathiae - erysipeloid of Rosenbach (subacute cellulitis of the fingers/hand).
c) Treatment: Aeromonas - fluoroquinolone or third-gen cephalosporin +/- doxycycline; B. pseudomallei - ceftazidime or a carbapenem (meropenem) then eradication with TMP-SMX; V. vulnificus - third-gen cephalosporin + doxycycline (or fluoroquinolone) plus surgical debridement; S. iniae - penicillin/beta-lactam; M. marinum - clarithromycin plus ethambutol +/- rifampin; E. rhusiopathiae - penicillin or ampicillin.
d) Prophylaxis (wound exposure): no firm guideline; irrigate/debride, ensure tetanus prophylaxis, and consider empiric coverage for high-risk wounds (deep punctures, immunocompromised/liver disease) - e.g. a fluoroquinolone or first-gen cephalosporin, adding doxycycline for salt-water exposure to cover Vibrio and metronidazole for soil/sewage contamination.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only V. vulnificus is covered in this chapter; the other five pathogens' water exposure, syndromes, treatment and wound prophylaxis are from established knowledge/IDSA SSTI and species-specific chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Water type: Aeromonas - fresh water; Burkholderia pseudomallei - fresh water; Vibrio vulnificus - salt water; Streptococcus iniae - fresh water; Mycobacterium marinum - salt or fresh water; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - salt water. Clinical: Aeromonas - cellulitis/myonecrosis/rhabdo/ecthyma gangrenosum, men:women 3:1, also leech-associated; Burkholderia pseudomallei - melioidosis, intracellular GNB, skin ulcers/abscesses failing PO abx, worse in cirrhotics; Vibrio vulnificus - rapidly progressive infection, necrotizing infections, hemorrhagic bullae, linked to raw oysters/puncture wounds; Streptococcus iniae - assoc with tilapia fish farming, impetigo/cellulitis; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - erysipeloid of Rosenbach, subacute cellulitis of fingers/hands; Mycobacterium marinum - indolent (mean incubation 21d), papules/nodules progressing to ulceration/scar, sporotrichoid spread. Treatment: Aeromonas – Doxycycline + FQ/3rd gen Ceph; Burkholderia pseudomallei – Ceftazidime or carbapenem; Vibrio vulnificus – Doxycycline + 3rd gen ceph; Streptococcus iniae – beta-lactam; Mycobacterium marinum – Clarithromycin + Ethambutol/Rifampin; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae – penicillin/ampicillin/cephalexin. Prophylaxis: no clear guideline; reasonable for deep puncture/laceration, wounds needing surgical repair, wounds with water exposure outside treated pools, crush injury, vascular/lymphatic compromise, hands/feet/face/genital area, near bone/joint, immunocompromised/diabetic/liver disease. Empiric: 1st gen cephalosporin OR clindamycin + fluoroquinolone; salt water add doxycycline; soil/sewage add metronidazole; wash wound, debride, tetanus prophylaxis
